questions.scenario: Marden & Vale's bid team uses Claude to produce first-draft tender responses. A bid manager has noticed that the drafts are usually excellent in substance but the numbers in the commercial table are frequently wrong — often plausible-looking figures that don't match the pricing workbook.
questions.stem: The team has already confirmed the workbook is attached and the instructions say to use the pricing schedule. What is the MOST likely cause and the best next step?

options.text: The pricing table is being reconstructed from memory across a long conversation, so ask Claude to re-read the pricing schedule immediately before producing the table and to state the source cell for each figure.
The instructions are too long, so reduce them to the three rules that matter most and the numbers will follow.
Switch to a more capable model, since the errors are arithmetic and precision-driven.
Ask Claude to flag any figure it is not certain about so the bid team can check those before submission.

questions.explanation: The symptom is **specific**: substance is right, figures are wrong. That points at how the numbers are being produced rather than at capability or instructions. A long conversation is full of earlier, different numbers, and generating a table of figures is exactly the kind of task where a plausible-looking wrong value is more likely than an obvious error. Re-reading the source immediately before the table, and being required to name where each figure came from, forces the answer to be traceable rather than composed.

whyWrong.B: Instruction length is not the differentiator here — the narrative sections are consistently good, so the model is following the instructions. Shortening them is unlikely to change how numbers are produced.
whyWrong.C: A more capable model will still produce a table. The issue is that composing figures is being asked of it at all, at a point in the conversation where the authoritative values are far back.
whyWrong.D: Flagging uncertainty is a mitigation, not a fix. Every figure sounds equally certain, and it still leaves the bid team checking numbers one by one.

questions.mindset: Read the symptom: right substance, wrong specifics usually means the specifics are being generated rather than looked up.

questions.scenario: Redhaven Renewables' reporting analyst asks Claude to summarise the 90-page annual grid-connection report. She has received summaries that are fluent and well organised but occasionally contradict the source — for example stating a connection date that the report gives differently two pages later.
questions.stem: What is the MOST likely explanation for the contradictions?

options.text: The whole document was compressed into one pass, so details far apart in the text get blended; ask for section-by-section work with the section named, and spot-check a sample of claims against the source.
The model cannot handle 90 pages, so the summary should be limited to the first 20 pages.
The document is too long for the model's context window, so it is silently summarising only what fitted.
The analyst's prompt is ambiguous about length, so add a word count to force a tighter summary.

questions.explanation: Contradictions that appear *only* in specifics, while structure and tone stay good, are the classic signature of compressing a long document in one pass: the summary is built from a blended impression rather than from located facts. Working **section by section with the section identified** keeps each claim tied to where it came from, and spot-checking a sample is what turns 'looks right' into evidence that it is right.

whyWrong.B: Truncating to 20 pages guarantees that most of the report is unsummarised. The problem is how the summarisation is done, not how much is covered.
whyWrong.C: 90 pages fits comfortably. If content were being dropped for space you would expect visible gaps and repeated apologies, not confident detail that contradicts itself.
whyWrong.D: A word limit compresses the output; it does not change how the input is processed. The contradictions would simply be fewer and shorter.

questions.mindset: Contradictions in detail with clean structure means the content was compressed, not read closely.

questions.scenario: At Fenmoor Group, an analyst's summaries have come back ignoring the instruction to focus on cash flow. She has tried rephrasing twice, with the same result. She then notices that the document heading itself is 'Results and Outlook', so almost every paragraph is about revenue and profit.
questions.stem: What is the BEST diagnosis and next step?

options.text: The input doesn't support the request: almost nothing in the document is about cash flow, so ask for a summary of what the document does say, then source cash-flow figures from the right report.
The instruction needs to be at the very start of the message rather than the end, so move it and try once more.
Add 'This is CRITICAL' in capitals before the cash-flow instruction to make sure it is followed.
Ask Claude to repeat the instruction back to confirm it understood before summarising.

questions.explanation: Two rephrasings producing the same result is the signal to stop rewriting the prompt and check the **input**. Claude is faithfully summarising a document about revenue and profit; there is no cash-flow content to focus on. The right move is to name that mismatch, summarise what is actually there, and get the cash-flow numbers from the statement of cash flows — a different document. Re-rolling the wording cannot create information that isn't present.

whyWrong.B: Position matters less than this suggests, and the failure has survived two substantial rewrites. When phrasing stops helping, the cause is upstream of phrasing.
whyWrong.C: Emphasis is not information. The model cannot emphasise cash flow in a document that does not discuss it, and shouting usually produces a cosmetic change.
whyWrong.D: Confirming comprehension is a reasonable check in general, but it tests the model's reading of the instruction, not whether the document supports the request.

questions.mindset: When two rewrites change nothing, stop editing the prompt and check whether the input can support the request at all.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Care's HR team asked Claude to draft offer letters from a template, and the first ten letters were fine. Since then the team has been getting letters that skip the paragraph about the probation review, and nobody changed the template.
questions.stem: Which explanation BEST fits this pattern, and what is the BEST response?

options.text: Output varies between runs even with the same input, so the fix is to remove the variation: put the required section order and the probation paragraph into the instructions and provide one approved example letter.
The template must have been altered by someone, so restore it from the previous version and re-run.
The team has been copying different parts of the letter into their requests, which is confusing the model; ask everyone to send the template in full each time.
The instruction is too long, so trim it to the three most important requirements and test on ten more letters.

questions.explanation: Nobody changed the input, and the output still changed — that is the signature of **non-determinism**, not of a broken template. Same-input-different-output is expected behaviour, so the fix is to remove the degrees of freedom: state the required structure explicitly and give one approved example, which is the most reliable way to pin format and content. Retrying until you get a good letter is the same problem with extra steps.

whyWrong.B: There is no evidence the template changed, and even if it had, the described symptom is variability between runs of an unchanged template.
whyWrong.C: Plausible as a cause but it doesn't fit the timeline — the pattern started without any change in how people were asking.
whyWrong.D: Trimming helps readability but doesn't pin structure. An explicit section list plus a worked example does.

questions.mindset: Unchanged input with changing output means non-determinism — remove the variability with structure and an example.

questions.scenario: Ivybridge College's admissions team gives Claude a transcript and a course entry requirement, and asks whether the applicant meets it. Replies are inconsistent: some say clearly yes, others hedge heavily with 'it appears the applicant may partially meet the requirement'.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective improvement to the request?

options.text: Define the decision and its options explicitly — meet, not meet, or insufficient information — with a rule for what evidence counts as meeting each requirement.
Ask for a confidence score between 1 and 10 alongside each answer, so the team can sort the borderline cases.
Ask Claude to be decisive and avoid hedging, so the team gets clear answers.
Add the requirement text to the prompt again, in case it was overlooked.

questions.explanation: The hedging is not caution — it is a **missing decision boundary**. The request leaves three legitimate outcomes open without saying how to tell them apart, so the model invents its own boundary each time. Naming the allowed outcomes, and the evidence required for each, converts a vague judgement into a defined one — and 'insufficient information' becomes a legitimate answer rather than something the model has to hedge around.

whyWrong.B: A self-assessed confidence number is not a reliable accuracy signal, and it doesn't stop the underlying vagueness — the same case would be scored differently on another run.
whyWrong.C: Asking for decisiveness suppresses the symptom while removing the ambiguity that caused it. The model will simply sound confident about a judgement it still has no criteria for.
whyWrong.D: Repeating the requirement adds no new information. The ambiguity is in what counts as evidence, not in whether the requirement was read.

questions.mindset: Hedging means the decision boundary was never defined. Name the options and what counts as each.

questions.scenario: At Silverbrook Foods, a packaging team reports four separate complaints about the same Claude Project in one week: summaries too long, summaries too short, the wrong tone for a retailer audience, and a request for a specific claim the labels aren't allowed to make. A colleague proposes adding 'Be concise, thorough, professional and compliant' to the instructions.
questions.stem: Which TWO problems with that proposal are the MOST important? Choose TWO.

options.text: Four complaints about opposite things are not one problem to average — they suggest the instructions never defined length, tone or claim boundaries for each output type.
'Concise, thorough, professional and compliant' is a list of abstract adjectives that gives Claude nothing concrete to act on, and 'concise' and 'thorough' pull against each other.
Four complaints in a week is far too many, so the team should wait for more evidence before changing anything.
The tone complaint suggests the model is unsuitable for retail audiences and the work should move to a different tool.

questions.explanation: **A** is the diagnosis that matters: complaints in opposite directions aren't a problem to be averaged, they're evidence that nothing was specified. Different output types need different targets — a retailer summary and a internal QA summary shouldn't share a length rule. **B** is why the proposed fix fails: 'concise' and 'thorough' are opposites presented as a solution, and adjectives like 'professional' and 'compliant' have no observable meaning to act on. Concrete targets — under 80 words, third person, claims only from the approved claims sheet — actually change the output.

whyWrong.C: Four distinct complaints in a week is plenty of evidence to act on. Waiting for more only means more unusable packaging drafts.
whyWrong.D: One audience complaint says nothing about the model's suitability. Tone is set by instructions describing the audience, which is a fixable configuration gap.

questions.mindset: Opposite complaints mean nothing was specified; adjective lists hide that instead of fixing it.

questions.scenario: A logistics account manager wrote: 'These summaries still don't land with the customer.' The summaries currently list operational facts — delivery times, pallet counts, incident logs — and end with a paragraph about ongoing improvements.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to use this feedback?

options.text: Ask which specific part of the summary fails to land and what the customer needs to act on, then rewrite the structure so the commercial point and the ask come first and the operational detail supports them.
Rewrite the summary to be shorter, on the assumption that the problem is length.
Ask Claude to suggest three different structures for the next summary and send all three to the customer.
Add 'Make the summary more customer-focused' to the Project instructions.

questions.explanation: 'Don't land' names a symptom, not a cause. The useful move is to convert it into something checkable: which part, and what does the reader need to do differently? The likely mismatch is **emphasis** — operational detail is present but the commercial point and the ask are buried at the end — and that is a structural change you can make and test. Feedback you can act on beats feedback you can only rephrase.

whyWrong.B: Length is a guess. Cutting words from a summary whose commercial point is last makes it shorter without making it land.
whyWrong.C: Offering the customer three structures transfers your editorial decision to them and makes the deliverable look unfinished.
whyWrong.D: 'More customer-focused' is an abstract goal with no observable behaviour attached, so it changes nothing reliably.

questions.mindset: Turn vague feedback into a specific, testable change before you rewrite anything.

questions.scenario: At Halcyon Legal, the litigation team ran two experiments on the same contract-review prompt: one added 'be thorough', the other supplied a worked example of a good review. The example produced markedly better and more consistent reviews.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful conclusion for the team's practice?

options.text: When feedback is about output quality, an example of good output is usually more effective than an adjective asking for more of something, because it fixes both the target and the format.
Adjectives like 'thorough' are unreliable and should never be used in prompts.
The team should run every prompt change against a worked example to be sure of results.
Since the example worked, the team should stop testing prompt variants altogether.

questions.explanation: The finding is consistent with the documented guidance that **examples are the most effective tool for controlling format, tone and structure**, and more reliable than abstract descriptions. 'Be thorough' doesn't say what thorough looks like, so it can be satisfied in several ways — which is likely why results were inconsistent. The example defines the target concretely, so a reviewer can tell whether it was met.

whyWrong.B: Too strong. Adjectives aren't useless; they're just weak where the standard is not self-evident. 'Under 200 words' or 'name the clause and the risk' work well.
whyWrong.C: Over-generalised from one case. Examples are powerful but not universal — for factual accuracy, a source-grounding rule is what's needed.
whyWrong.D: One successful change is a reason to keep testing, not to stop. The next output type may respond differently.

questions.mindset: To define a standard you can't name, show an example of it rather than asking for it with an adjective.

questions.scenario: Redhaven Renewables' team ran a prompt change that improved output on their 30 test requests but, on live work, produced longer responses that executives found harder to read.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to respond to the conflicting signals?

options.text: Find out how the test set differs from live work — audience, length expectations, or how much context real requests carry — and fix the gap before deciding whether the change was an improvement.
Keep the change, because the test set was larger and more systematic than anecdote about a few executives.
Revert the change, since real users are the ultimate measure of quality.
Split the difference by keeping the change for internal audiences and asking Claude to shorten output for executive audiences.

questions.explanation: Two disagreeing signals usually mean the **test doesn't represent the work**, not that the tool is unreliable. Before choosing a side, find the difference: test prompts with a fixed length and no executive audience don't exercise the constraint that broke. Checking that gap is cheap and turns the conflict into a concrete change — and it stops a team from reverting a real improvement because its test set was unrepresentative.

whyWrong.B: Sample size isn't the issue if the test set doesn't cover the case that matters. Thirty unrepresentative requests can be more misleading than three well-observed ones.
whyWrong.C: Reverting throws away a genuine improvement and leaves the underlying test-set gap unaddressed, so the next change will fail the same way.
whyWrong.D: Prompting for brevity doesn't fix a test gap, and audience-conditional length rules accumulate quickly into conflicting instructions.

questions.mindset: When test results and real results disagree, suspect the test set before you pick a side.

questions.scenario: Calder & Sons found that quote drafts were repeatedly coming back with the wrong scaffold type specified. Two colleagues fixed it differently: one added a line to the Project instructions saying to confirm the scaffold type with the surveyor before quoting; the other added an instruction naming the four scaffold types and how to tell them apart from the survey photos.
questions.stem: Which approach is likely to hold up better on unseen quotes, and why?

options.text: The second: it gives Claude the discriminating information it was missing, so it can identify the type from the evidence rather than relying on someone remembering to ask.
The first: asking for confirmation moves the check to a person who can authorise it, which is always more reliable.
Both are equivalent, and the team should keep whichever is shorter.
Neither will hold up, because the real fix is to stop Claude from producing quotes at all.

questions.explanation: The first approach depends on a **human step happening every time**, which is exactly the kind of thing that gets skipped under deadline. The second supplies what Claude was missing — how to distinguish the four types from the evidence — so it can do the work itself and apply the reasoning to cases nobody anticipated. Where you can close an information gap, close it, rather than building a process that depends on vigilance.

whyWrong.B: Asking for confirmation is a reasonable safety net, but it can't help on the many quotes where nobody notices a problem and so never confirms. It also slows every quote down.
whyWrong.C: The two are not equivalent: one adds knowledge, the other adds a dependency on human behaviour that decays under time pressure.
whyWrong.D: Wrong type errors are a fixable information gap, not a reason to remove a capability the business depends on.

questions.mindset: Prefer closing the information gap over adding a step that depends on people remembering under pressure.

questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics has run the same weekly dispatch report for a year. Users report that it became verbose and repetitive roughly six months ago, and nobody changed the instructions.
questions.stem: What is the MOST likely explanation and the BEST response?

options.text: Users have probably been adding their own formatting requests in chat to compensate, and those accumulated requests are now shaping the output; look at recent chats, then move the recurring ones into the Project instructions.
The report has become verbose because the model has learned the organisation's preferred style, which is a form of drift that can only be corrected by starting a fresh Project.
Add a length limit to the instructions and ask users to stop adding their own formatting requests in future.
Switch to a different model, since verbosity of this kind indicates the current model is being over-fitted by the organisation's usage.

questions.explanation: A gradual change with no configuration change is usually caused by **users adapting to the tool** — adding 'keep it short', 'use bullets' or 'skip the good news' in individual chats until the report's shape is being decided in a dozen places instead of one. Chat-level instructions accumulate and shape later output, so the durable fix is to find the recurring ones and promote them into the Project instructions, where they are visible and maintainable.

whyWrong.B: Models do not learn from usage. Nothing here requires a new Project, and discarding the accumulated context loses the setup that works.
whyWrong.C: Blaming users for adding instructions doesn't remove the instructions, and a length limit in the Project competes with chat-level requests rather than replacing them.
whyWrong.D: Over-fitting from usage isn't a model behaviour. Switching models would reset the context and lose whatever accumulated structure is helping.

questions.mindset: Behaviour that drifts without a config change usually drifted because people adapted in chat. Promote their workarounds.

questions.scenario: Fernwood Legal's intake team handles about 25 enquiries a day, each needing a summary of the enquiry, a conflict check, and a proposed next step. Today each enquiry is started as a fresh chat with everything retyped.
questions.stem: Which change would MOST improve efficiency while keeping quality?

options.text: Build a Project that holds the firm's intake procedure and the standard conflict-check questions as knowledge, so each enquiry needs only its own facts typed in.
Have one person handle all 25 enquiries in a single continuous chat, so nothing has to be re-explained.
Write a saved prompt containing the intake procedure and paste it into each new chat.
Ask the team to type more detail up front so Claude needs fewer follow-up questions.

questions.explanation: The waste is **retyping the same material** into every chat: the procedure and the standard questions are identical each time. A Project stores them once and applies them to every chat, which removes the repetition and — because the procedure lives in one place — makes it consistent and easy to update. That's the same reasoning as storing reusable material in knowledge rather than in each conversation.

whyWrong.B: One chat for 25 enquiries accumulates history that is carried into every message, uses the allowance faster and makes earlier matters harder to separate from current ones.
whyWrong.C: A saved prompt still has to be pasted every time and can be used inconsistently. It's an improvement on retyping the procedure, but the material isn't stored once — it's copied repeatedly, which invites drift.
whyWrong.D: More typing up front adds effort to every case rather than removing the repetition, and it puts the burden on the people who are already behind.

questions.mindset: If the same material is retyped into every conversation, store it once where it applies automatically.

questions.scenario: Torrington Water's team has a Project that answers staff questions about the annual water-quality report. It works well. A colleague notices that most questions are answered from three short sections of the report, and the whole 200-page document is being carried in the Project's knowledge.
questions.stem: Which optimisation is MOST likely to help, and why?

options.text: Leave it as it is, because reducing the knowledge would risk answers going stale or incomplete.
Test whether most questions are answerable from the sections staff actually ask about, and if so consider a smaller curated knowledge set plus the full document linked for depth.
Move the full report into the instructions so it is always read in full before answering.
Delete the full report and rely on Claude's general knowledge about water quality for anything not covered.

questions.explanation: The disciplined way to optimise context is **measure first**: identify what the knowledge is actually used for, then curate toward that. If nearly all questions come from a few sections, a smaller authoritative set answers them with less to wade through, while keeping the full report available for depth preserves the long tail. What must not happen is an untested trim — removing material on a hunch is what turns an optimisation into a regression.

whyWrong.A: Defensive inaction is a choice, not a default. Context that isn't being used is a real cost on every request in the Project.
whyWrong.C: Instructions are for behaviour, not reference content. Putting a 200-page report there guarantees it is loaded on every interaction and buries any actual rules.
whyWrong.D: This trades a verification problem for a hallucination problem. Nothing in general knowledge substitutes for the utility's own measurements.

questions.mindset: Optimise context from evidence about what's used, never from a guess about what might be needed.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Care's rota team builds 200 weekly staff schedules with Claude. Each schedule has taken about 40 minutes of manual tidying after the draft, because Claude's output mixes the clinical cover requirement into the narrative notes.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST reduce that manual tidying? Choose TWO.

options.text: Define the output as a table with fixed named columns, so the clinical cover requirement has a defined place to go instead of appearing in prose.
Build the rota by having Claude produce a plain narrative and let a person restructure it, since narrative output is more reliable.
Ask Claude to check each finished draft against the cover rules and list any breaches before it is used.
Add 'make the output cleaner and better organised' to the Project instructions.
Process all 200 schedules in a single batch so the format settles across them.

questions.explanation: The 40 minutes is **reformatting and verification**, so those are the two things to remove. **A** gives the cover requirement a defined column so it stops landing in prose, which is where the tidying comes from. **C** moves the correctness check into the process: listing breaches before use turns a manual read-through into a short list to review. Structure plus a self-check addresses both halves of what the person is doing.

whyWrong.B: Keeping the manual restructuring step and merely changing the wording keeps the 40 minutes exactly where it is — it's a reorganisation of the input, not a removal of the work.
whyWrong.D: 'Cleaner and better organised' has no observable definition, so it can't change the output structure reliably. It's the abstract version of the concrete fix in A.
whyWrong.E: Batching the volume doesn't address the format problem and risks losing per-schedule quality attention across 200 cases.

questions.mindset: Measure where the manual time actually goes, then remove that step with structure or a check — not adjectives.

questions.scenario: A team lead reviews four colleagues' Claude workflows and finds: one retypes a standard brief every time; one keeps a year-long chat open for everything; one pastes the same 80-page manual into each new chat; one uses a Project with the manual as knowledge and specific instructions.
questions.stem: Which TWO of these are creating avoidable waste? Choose TWO.

options.text: The one retyping a standard brief, because the brief is identical each time and could live in the Project's instructions.
The one keeping a year-long chat open, because every message carries the whole history forward, using allowance faster and making early decisions harder to surface.
The one pasting the manual into each new chat, because the same 80 pages are re-uploaded rather than stored once.
The one using a Project with the manual as knowledge, because Projects are slower than plain chats.

questions.explanation: Two are wasting effort and two are fine. A year-long chat and repeated 80-page uploads are the two classic hidden costs: the first carries all prior history into every message, and the second re-sends the same bulk content conversation after conversation. The Project setup in D is the efficient pattern — knowledge stored once, instructions applied automatically — and plain chats aren't inherently faster in any way that matters for this work.

whyWrong.A: Retyping a standard brief is tedious but it's a short, bounded cost, and keeping the brief visible in the request can be a deliberate way to confirm it each time. The two costs flagged here are the ones that scale with conversation length.
whyWrong.D: This inverts the pattern. Storing the manual once as project knowledge is precisely what removes the repeat upload, and Projects exist to apply instructions consistently across every chat.

questions.mindset: The waste that scales is long histories and repeated bulk uploads — store once, summarise and restart.

questions.scenario: Silverbrook Foods switched a Project from a more capable model to a faster, cheaper one to reduce costs. Cost fell by 60%. Six weeks later, the complaints team reports that escalation emails are longer, more hedged, and miss the customer's actual issue more often.
questions.stem: What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Use the faster model for routine work and route the escalation email type back to the more capable model, since the complaints have identified where the capability gap actually shows up.
Move every task back to the more capable model, since the complaints suggest it is unreliable across the board.
Keep the faster model everywhere and add more rules to the instructions describing what a good escalation email looks like.
Keep the faster model and accept the complaints, since the cost saving funds the rest of the team's usage.

questions.explanation: The complaints are **evidence about where capability matters**, and they point at one output type rather than all of them. That supports routing: keep the saving where it's working and spend it back where judgement and tone are load-bearing. It's the same discipline as testing before switching — the cost figure was measured, and now the quality figure is telling you which tasks can carry the cheaper model.

whyWrong.B: Over-corrects from one symptom. Routine work was presumably fine on the faster model, so reverting everything gives back the saving without fixing the diagnosis.
whyWrong.C: More instructions can help with structure but won't add the judgement the complaints describe. If the capability gap is real, wording is the wrong instrument.
whyWrong.D: Trading away the quality of customer-facing escalations for usage budget is a decision to make explicitly with the business, not to take by default and hope nobody objects.

questions.mindset: When a cheaper model causes specific quality problems, route by task type rather than reverting or ignoring.

questions.scenario: Rookwood Energy's project office produces a weekly progress report. Claude's draft is good, but the office manager spends 20 minutes each week copying key points into the team's reporting template and emailing it onward.
questions.stem: Which change would MOST reduce that 20 minutes?

options.text: Have Claude produce the report directly in the required template format, with the section headings and field names the team already uses.
Ask Claude to output a shorter report so there is less to copy into the template.
Switch to a faster model so the report arrives sooner and can be copied while still fresh.
Add an instruction telling the office manager not to alter the wording of Claude's report before sending it.

questions.explanation: The 20 minutes is a **format mismatch**: the content is right and the shape is wrong, so someone is translating between the two every week. Producing the output in the target format eliminates the translation step entirely. Shortening the report doesn't help — the manager still has to find each item and place it in the template — and speed isn't the constraint, since the copying happens regardless of how quickly the draft arrives.

whyWrong.B: Fewer words in the wrong shape still require the same manual placement. The cost here is structural, not volumetric.
whyWrong.C: Faster delivery doesn't remove a step that happens after the draft is complete.
whyWrong.D: This forbids the editing the manager does precisely because the format doesn't match, without addressing why it doesn't match.

questions.mindset: When someone is reformatting your output, hand over the shape they need, not the same content again.

questions.scenario: Halcyon Legal's knowledge team maintains Projects for six practice areas. Each Project's instructions have grown to 40-60 lines. New matters take longer to get right because people keep adding local rules in chat, and reviewers can't tell which rules are live.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST improve this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Prune each Project's instructions to the rules that demonstrably change output, moving reference material into knowledge, and test with known questions afterwards.
Merge all six practice areas into one Project with all the instructions in order of importance, so people only have to remember one place.
Require new rules to be added to the Project instructions rather than to individual chats, so the rules live in one reviewable place.
Number every existing rule so reviewers can refer to them precisely in feedback.
Move all six practice areas' reference material into a single shared folder that every Project links to.

questions.explanation: The two problems are **noise** and **diffuse ownership of rules**, so both must be attacked. **A** removes the lines that don't earn their place and moves reference content out of where behaviour should be defined, then confirms nothing broke. **C** gives the rules a single home, which is what makes them reviewable — a rule typed into one person's chat helps one matter and disappears, while a rule in the instructions applies to every matter in that practice area.

whyWrong.B: Merging compounds the problem: one Project with six practice areas' instructions has all the noise and none of the scoping. People would still not know which rules apply to their matter.
whyWrong.D: Numbering helps people cite rules but does nothing about there being 60 of them, or about the ones that are obsolete or contradictory.
whyWrong.E: A single shared reference folder across six practice areas mixes unrelated material and creates one more thing to curate, without touching the instruction bloat.

questions.mindset: Fix instruction bloat by pruning to what changes output, and keep rules in the one place they can be reviewed.
